title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Starting point
AI system and date: ChatGPT, 11/9/2026
Before using AI for the required extension, briefly state your question, course-based core model, baseline result, and the specific limitation or opportunity you wanted to address.

Our question is how is the amount spent on healthcare related to age, sex, BMI, number of children, smoking status, and region of the United States you life in? We are using a multiple linear regression model. The baseline result is that smoking, BMI, number of children, and age all are associated with significant changes in yearly healthcare charges. We wanted to see which predictors were the most important in predicting healthcare charges. Though we could use a best-subsets selection or use the VIFs of each variable to get an idea of which matters most, we wanted to directly compare each variable’s importance on the same baseline. A model selection search will tell us which variables should be included, but not rank and measure their importance.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Independent verification

If our extension shows that smoking, age, and BMI are significantly more important than the other predictors, than a LASSO shrinkage should reasonably select those same predictors.



Show code
# Code to import data, for reference
library(tidyverse)
library(vroom)
library(broom)
# insurance.csv is from
# https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/d3lhomi10/medical-cost-personal-dataset
insurance_data <- vroom("insurance.csv") %>% 
  mutate(across(c(sex, smoker, region), as.factor))
insurance_fit <- lm(charges ~ ., data = insurance_data)
insurance_data$bmi_group <- as.factor(cut(
  insurance_data$bmi,
  breaks = c(0, 25, 30, Inf),
  labels = c("Normal", "Overweight", "Obese")
))

library(glmnet)
# make a model matrix and remove the intercept column
x <- model.matrix(charges ~ . - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)[, -1]
y <- insurance_data$charges

# do a lasso regression (alpha = 1)
lasso <- cv.glmnet(x, y, family = "gaussian", alpha = 1)
coef(lasso)

This lasso regression keeps the coefficients for age, bmi, and smoker. This checks that the AI’s importance ranking is correct. The LASSO regression also gave smoker the largest coefficient, which matches the AI response that smoker is the most important coefficient. However, this check also shows why a LASSO regression or other model selection method is not sufficient for ranking the importance of coefficients, because age and bmi are given almost the same final coefficient whereas the actual importance ranking puts age significantly above bmi. Because the coefficients are not all on the same scale, we cannot simply compare them to see which matters most for prediction, though smoker being much larger than age and bmi points towards it being the most important coefficient.

We can use \(R^2\) to explore which variables are the most important. We can fit partial models, each one dropping one of our predictors, and see how much the \(R^2\) drops when we drop each variable.



Show code
partial1 <- lm(charges ~ . - age - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial2 <- lm(charges ~ . - sex - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial3<- lm(charges ~ . - bmi - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial4 <- lm(charges ~ . - children - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial5 <- lm(charges ~ . - smoker - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)
partial6 <- lm(charges ~ . - region - bmi_group, data = insurance_data)

adj.r.squareds <- c(
    glance(partial1)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial2)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial3)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial4)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial5)$adj.r.squared,
    glance(partial6)$adj.r.squared
)

r.squareds <- tibble(
    model = c("Age", "Sex", "BMI", "Children", "Smoker", "Region"),
    adj.r.squared.delta = glance(insurance_fit)$adj.r.squared - adj.r.squareds
)
knitr::kable(r.squareds)

This table lists the change in adjusted \(R^2\), where a positive number means a drop in adjusted \(R^2\). Omitting each of the variables caused a drop in \(R^2\) except for sex, however the drop due to omitting region, children, and sex were all very small (<.003). This also reinforces the AI work, showing that age, BMI, and especially smoker have a significant impact on the predictions. \(R^2\) is also nice because it is quantifiable. The change in \(R^2\) is the change in the percentage of variation that the model explains. So, we can see that removing smoker causes the amount of variation explained to drop by nearly 63%, removing age and bmi cause the amount of explained variation to drop by about 9% and 3% respectively, while removing sex, children, or region only cause a drop of less than .3% each, or even an increase in the case of sex.

title: Health Insurance Pricing
text:
The question
In one or two short paragraphs, introduce the setting, audience, focused research question, data source, observational unit, response, important predictors, and one important data limitation. Lead with what makes the question worth answering.
How is the amount spent on healthcare related to age, sex, BMI, number of children, smoking status, and region of the United States you life in? This study is for those setting health insurance pricing so that they can better understand the effect of these factors on the amount of health insurance a policyholder will need. Understanding these relationships can help insurance companies make more informed decisions when determining insurance premiums and help policyholders identify factors associated with higher healthcare costs. The data comes from the insurance.csv dataset, originally published in Brett Lantz’s Machine Learning with R and available through Kaggle. The observational unit is one individual, with a total of 1,338 individuals and seven variables. The response variable is charges, which represents the total annual healthcare charges for each individual. The six candidate predictors are age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, and region.
We expect smoking status to be one of the strongest predictors of healthcare charges, with age and BMI also likely to have important associations. Identifying these relationships may help insurance companies better understand healthcare costs when setting premiums and help policyholders recognize factors associated with higher insurance expenses. However, an important limitation is that the dataset is observational and provides limited information about its original data collection process. Therefore, we can identify associations between these variables and healthcare charges, but we cannot conclude that any of these factors directly cause healthcare costs to increase or decrease.

It is clear from these plots that healthcare charges increase with age, and that smokers generally spend more per year for healthcare. BMI doesn’t seem to have as much of an effect as expected, however it seems to have an interaction with smoking status. Healthcare costs seem to stay mostly the same as BMI increases except for the group of individuals who are smokers and obese. Smokers in the normal and overweight BMI categories seem to be charged about $15000 more per year across the age levels recorded, but obese smokers are charged about $35000 more on average across all age levels.

Show code
# Implement the verified extension or show its most useful result.

library(tidymodels)

set.seed(502340)

folds <- vfold_cv(
  insurance_data,
  v = 10,
  repeats = 5
)

# Predictors to investigate
predictors <- c(
  "age",
  "sex",
  "bmi",
  "children",
  "smoker",
  "region"
)

# Number of random permutations
n_permutations <- 30

# Calculate permutation importance

importance_results <- map2_dfr(
  folds$splits,
  seq_along(folds$splits),

  function(split, i) {

    # Separate training and assessment observations
    train_data <- analysis(split)
    test_data <- assessment(split)

    # Fit regression using training observations
    model <- lm(
      charges ~ age + sex + bmi +
        children + smoker + region,
      data = train_data
    )

    # Original predictions and RMSE
    original_predictions <- predict(
      model,
      newdata = test_data
    )

    original_rmse <- rmse_vec(
      truth = test_data$charges,
      estimate = original_predictions
    )

    # Shuffle each predictor independently
    map_dfr(
      predictors,

      function(variable) {

        shuffled_rmse <- replicate(
          n_permutations,

          {
            shuffled_data <- test_data

            shuffled_data[[variable]] <-
              sample(shuffled_data[[variable]])

            predictions <- predict(
              model,
              newdata = shuffled_data
            )

            rmse_vec(
              truth = test_data$charges,
              estimate = predictions
            )
          }
        )

        tibble(
          fold = folds$id[i],
          repeat_id = folds$id2[i],
          variable = variable,
          original_rmse = original_rmse,
          permutation = seq_len(n_permutations),
          shuffled_rmse = shuffled_rmse,
          importance = shuffled_rmse - original_rmse
        )
      }
    )
  }
)


importance_summary <- importance_results %>%
  group_by(variable) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_importance = mean(importance),
    sd_importance = sd(importance),
    median_importance = median(importance),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_importance))

first_split <- folds$splits[[1]]

train_check <- analysis(first_split)
test_check <- assessment(first_split)

check_model <- lm(
  charges ~ age + sex + bmi +
    children + smoker + region,
  data = train_check
)

check_predictions <- predict(
  check_model,
  newdata = test_check
)

# Method 1: yardstick
rmse_package <- rmse_vec(
  truth = test_check$charges,
  estimate = check_predictions
)

# Method 2: manual calculation
rmse_manual <- sqrt(
  mean(
    (test_check$charges -
